items.title: D-Day: The Final 72 Hours | As It Happened
items.description:
How close was D-Day to being called off? How did the Allies deceive the Germans? Was Omaha beach that bloody? Dan Snow and D-Day expert Stephen Fisher discuss the nail-biting 72 hours before and during D-Day - the largest seaborne invasion in history. 

This episode was made in partnership with STUDIOCANAL UK for their new film PRESSURE which tells this incredible untold story of Group Captain James Stagg, the man who delivered the most important weather forecast of all time. 

'Pressure' is out
items.why_watch: Dan Snow and D-Day historian Stephen Fisher walk through the 72 hours surrounding the Normandy landings with the pacing of a thriller — focusing on how genuinely close the operation came to being scrubbed due to weather, and how the Allied deception campaign kept the Germans paralyzed. At 87 minutes it's a commitment, but it rewards viewers who want real operational detail rather than highlight-reel heroics.

items.title: I time travelled to the Battle of Marathon 490BC #ancientgreece
items.why_watch: Chloe uses a fun 'time traveler' framing to deliver sharp, specific context about the Battle of Marathon — including details that complicate the familiar legend — in under three minutes. It's a good example of how short-form history content can inform without dumbing down. Worth it if you've ever repeated the marathon origin story and wondered how much of it holds up.

global_silver_linings.title: 5 US Cities Hire Robot Called ‘Dax’ to Help Survey and Repair Sidewalks–Kids Love Him
global_silver_linings.snippet: Citizens across the nation have reported strange figures on city sidewalks. They’re white, short, and inhuman. But this unidentified rolling object comes in peace.
global_silver_linings.reason: Cities are finding creative, community-friendly ways to maintain public infrastructure, and the fact that children are delighted by the process is a sweet reminder that practical solutions can also spark curiosity and joy. When kids engage with their neighbourhoods this way, they grow up caring about the shared spaces around them.

global_silver_linings.reason: Teachers standing up collectively — and then finding humour in the moment — shows that educators still have the solidarity and spirit to advocate for themselves and, by extension, for their students. A profession that can laugh together under pressure is one that hasn't lost its heart.

discovery_articles.title: Paleontologists Discover a New Species of Ice Age Toad at the La Brea Tar Pits, Offering Clues About the Area's Ancient Climate
discovery_articles.snippet: The fossilized remains, recovered in 1929, were part of La Brea's relatively understudied amphibian collection. Since toads are cold-blooded and sensitive to environmental changes, the discovery can help researchers piece together past climate conditions
discovery_articles.ferns_note: These bones sat quietly in a collection drawer for nearly a century before anyone realized they belonged to a species entirely new to science — proof that Ice Age secrets are still hiding in plain sight. And because toads are exquisitely tuned to their environment, this one tiny creature is now rewriting what we know about ancient Los Angeles.

discovery_articles.title: Snails Can Make Their Slime Sticky, Slippery, Foamy or Hard Depending on Their Needs. Here's How They Tweak Their Multipurpose Mucus
discovery_articles.snippet: The critters can alter the proportions of calcium and collagen in the versatile substance, which changes the protein structure. The different textures can help snails glide, climb or protect themselves
discovery_articles.ferns_note: A snail's slime isn't just slime — it's a shapeshifting material the creature actively engineers, toggling between glue, grease, foam, and armor by adjusting its chemistry on the fly. It's the kind of quiet biological wizardry that makes you look twice at something you'd normally step around.

discovery_articles.title: 1,800 Volunteers Pull a 400-Ton Japanese Castle Keep Back Toward Its Original Location After a Decade of Restoration Work
discovery_articles.snippet: The chance to help move the castle keep drew thousands of applications from Japan and abroad. Groups of lottery winners took turns tugging on thick ropes attached to the massive structure
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Thousands of people from around the world entered a lottery for the chance to grip a rope and — just for a moment — become part of a 400-year-old castle's story. There's something deeply human about that: the urge to touch history rather than merely observe it.

discovery_articles.title: What Are Mel Brooks’ Favorite Movies? To Celebrate His 100th Birthday, the Comedy Legend Picks 20 Films to Screen Across Los Angeles
discovery_articles.snippet: The eclectic program spans decades and genres, offering glimpses into Brooks’ comedic influences, personal history and enduring love of film
discovery_articles.ferns_note: A century of living distilled into a 20-film playlist — Mel Brooks' picks are less a retrospective than a map of the mind that made us laugh for decades. Whatever he chose, the curation itself is the portrait.

discovery_articles.title: Tiny tremors can’t always warn when fracking will trigger a bigger quake
discovery_articles.snippet: A study of 70,000 earthquakes finds tiny tremors often precede larger fracking-linked quakes, offering a warning to halt fluid injection.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: The unsettling finding isn't that tiny tremors precede bigger fracking quakes — it's that they don't always, which means the early-warning system geologists were counting on has a troubling blind spot. Knowing the alarm sometimes stays silent is its own kind of alarm.

discovery_articles.title: Landslides pose the largest risks to those who can least afford them
discovery_articles.snippet: Appalachia is a hotspot of landslides, but many there can’t afford to move away or mitigate the danger, a new study finds. Wealthy urban residents can.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Landslides don't just strike indiscriminately — they tend to linger longest where people have the fewest options to leave, making geology and economic inequality a grimly predictable partnership. The mountain doesn't care about your zip code, but your zip code determines everything about what happens next.

discovery_articles.snippet: While bold in color, Ben Sledsens' oil-and-acrylic paintings are quiet and intimate. Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a Colossal Member today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Ben Sledsens paints with the volume turned all the way up in color, yet somehow the rooms and figures inside feel hushed — like catching a private moment through a very vivid window. It's a rare trick, and it works.

discovery_articles.title: ‘Handmade Utopia’ Relishes the Architecture of California’s Back-to-the-Land Movement
discovery_articles.snippet: The new book by David Jacob Kramer, with photos by Michael Schmelling, represents a counterculture that, though changed, is still alive and well. Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a Colossal Member today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: California's back-to-the-land movement was supposed to be a rejection of permanence, yet the handmade structures its dreamers left behind have outlasted the ideology — still standing, still inhabited, still quietly radical. This book suggests utopia, even a patched-together one, has a longer half-life than anyone expected.

news.title: The Easy Salad Dressing Recipe I Have Memorized (It’s That Good!)
news.snippet: No salad is complete without a good dressing. Since I started making my own salad dressings at home, I almost never buy them at the grocery store anymore. Making your own salad dressing is incredibly easy and budget-friendly, and I can guarantee that a homemade dressing is 10 times more flavorful than any store-bought one.
news.blurb: A gentle nudge to retire that dusty bottle from the fridge door — once you go homemade, there's truly no going back.

news.title: High in cocoa, high on nostalgia: the chocolate I love most now
news.snippet: Including, to my surprise, a 100% cacao bar … Although I’m un peu fatiguée of chocolates in bonbon shape with coloured cocoa-butter splashes atop, I appreciate this is the way many chocolates truffles are made. Overcoming that prejudice, I tucked into a box of Scoff chocolates. They were beautifully fresh tasting – they are made in batches throughout the year and the latest batch has just been let loose.
news.blurb: A beautifully opinionated tour through the cacao spectrum, from nostalgic comfort to the bracingly bold 100% bar, for anyone who takes their chocolate seriously.

fern_data.greeting: Late August light arrives already knowing it won't stay — which feels like the right morning to read about why your spine is quietly losing the argument with gravity, or to watch 1,800 volunteers inch a 400-ton Japanese castle keep back toward where it belongs.
